cases.title: Bandayi and Mege: houses demolished beside the Kibali gold mine
cases.place: Bandayi and Mege, Durba, Haut-Uélé, Democratic Republic of the Congo
cases.point: Coordinates are for Durba town, in Watsa territory, Haut-Uélé. Bandayi and Mege are the neighbourhoods next to the town; the parts that were demolished sat inside the area the Kibali mine calls Exclusion Zone B (PAX).

lenders.name: Barrick Gold Corporation (Canada), 45% owner and operator of Kibali Goldmines SA (foreign owner)
lenders.role: Runs the mine for the joint venture. It acquired the holding through its 2019 merger with Randgold (Canada's National Contact Point). PAX says Kibali repeatedly complained to the provincial and national governments about the people living in Exclusion Zone B, that the evictions would not have happened without Kibali's wish to use the land, and that Barrick's chief executive visited the mine less than ten days before the demolitions began.

lenders.name: AngloGold Ashanti plc (United Kingdom), 45% owner (foreign owner)
lenders.role: Holds 45% of Kibali Goldmines SA. It told the UK National Contact Point that Barrick operates the mine and that it does not manage day-to-day operations; the UK contact point said there was "significant leverage the Respondent could have had over the Mine" and its partners.

lenders.name: Société minière de Kilo-Moto (SOKIMO), 10% owner
lenders.role: Congolese state mining company, the third shareholder in the joint venture (PAX; UK National Contact Point; Reuters).

cases.conditions: The state cleared the land. No loan or aid condition was found; the outside money here is the two foreign owners' equity. PAX records a joint Kibali-provincial government workshop in January 2021 that recommended that the authorities demolish all unplanned buildings in the area the mine calls Exclusion Zone B, and a provincial decree of 9 March 2021 setting up a Special Demolition Commission to carry out the demolition plan. The demolitions were authorised by the governor of Haut-Uélé, supervised by the provincial mines minister and carried out by the Congolese army and the national police (Avocats Sans Frontières). The governor's office said in a statement reported by Reuters that the occupation of the two villages violated the rights of Kibali Goldmines.

companies.name: Barrick Gold Corporation
companies.role: 45% owner and operator of the Kibali mine
companies.desc: Canadian gold mining company, listed in New York and Toronto. Canada's National Contact Point records that it holds 45% of Kibali and operates the mine, an interest it got in the 2019 Randgold merger. PAX calls Kibali the largest gold mine in Africa.

companies.name: AngloGold Ashanti plc
companies.role: 45% owner of the Kibali mine; respondent to the complaints at the UK and United States contact points
companies.desc: Gold mining company. The UK National Contact Point records that it completed a corporate restructuring on 25 September 2023, giving it a corporate domicile in the UK and a primary listing of its ordinary shares on the New York Stock Exchange, and that it says Barrick runs the mine day to day. PAX describes it as based in the United Kingdom.

companies.name: Kibali Goldmines SA
companies.role: The joint venture company that owns the mine whose exclusion zone was cleared
companies.hq: Durba, Haut-Uélé, Democratic Republic of the Congo
companies.desc: Joint venture company incorporated under Congolese law, owned 45% by Barrick, 45% by AngloGold Ashanti and 10% by SOKIMO (UK National Contact Point). Its mining permits cover 1,836 square kilometres and it keeps a grievance office in Durba (PAX). It produced 364,000 ounces of gold in 2020, a company website figure reported by Reuters. Both complaints say security agents acted on Kibali's instruction, which the companies deny. Placed at Durba, the mine's town, as the documents give no registered-office address.

cases.community: Heavy machinery protected by state security forces demolished houses in Bandayi on 17, 18 and part of 19 October 2021 and in Mege on 20 and 21 October 2021. PAX puts the total at more than 2,500 houses pulled down by Congolese authorities, including the Special Demolition Commission, police and military, and estimates that about 2,500 households were left homeless, among them children, pregnant women and older people. A mission by three members of the national parliament, which visited Durba from 24 to 30 October 2021, counted 1,550 houses plus a nursery, a primary school and a secondary school in Bandayi, and 956 houses in Mege (PAX, reporting the parliamentary findings). Avocats Sans Frontières counts 953 structures destroyed in Mege alone on 19 and 20 October 2021 - 947 houses, one school, two shops and three churches - and says 610 victims who lost their homes and belongings were still without shelter, basic services and assistance a year later. Residents had minutes at most to take their belongings out, and houses were demolished with belongings inside when people were away (PAX). More than 2,360 households signed the complaints (OECD Watch).
cases.suppression: Residents of Durba tried to march to the authorities and to Kibali's community centre on 22 October 2021 and were blocked by police and military. State security forces fired tear gas and live ammunition. The parliamentary report found a disproportionate use of force and recorded fourteen people injured, among them a 13-year-old boy and a 17-year-old girl; protesters attacked public buildings, homes of police officers and police stations (PAX). Avocats Sans Frontières records more than fifteen people injured on 21 and 22 October, and afterwards arbitrary arrests, intimidation and attempted abductions of community leaders pressing the victims' claims. PAX reports that Congolese security forces arbitrarily arrested and mistreated people from Mege and Bandayi, in some cases holding them for several months, and that community members reported pressure, including death threats, to accept being called illegal occupants.
cases.killed_note: Three deaths are counted: protesters shot dead by Congolese state security forces at the Durba protest of 22 October 2021 against the demolitions. PAX, which read the parliamentary mission's report, says that report and annexed documents from health facilities record a soldier killed with a blunt object, at least three other people shot dead, and fourteen others injured; the report included four death certificates and photographs of the bodies. PAX's own summary says "the security forces fired live ammunition, killing at least three people" and that protesters killed a soldier on the same day. The soldier is not counted, because protesters killed him. The other three are counted because the forces that fired were the forces carrying out the demolition operation for the mine's exclusion zone: PAX records heavy machinery protected by state security forces and says the evictions followed lobbying by Kibali and Barrick, and Canada's National Contact Point recommended that Barrick disclose more about its relationship with local police and any arrangement to give material support to public security authorities. The counts differ between sources. Reuters, citing the Haut-Uélé governor's office, reported that "Shots were fired and at least one death and several wounded have been confirmed", without saying who fired. Mining.com, carrying a Reuters report, says the parliamentary mission found "four people, including one soldier, were shot dead and 14 others wounded". Avocats Sans Frontières gives at least four dead and more than fifteen injured in the repression of 21 and 22 October, without separating the soldier, so its four is the parliamentary four rather than a fourth death caused by the forces. Higher figures are not counted: the complainant told Canada's National Contact Point that six demonstrators were killed by police, Actualité.cd reported six dead on 23 October 2021, and PAX says it received reports of further dead protesters that it could not confirm. Barrick told Canada's National Contact Point that its understanding was that "two civilians and one police officer were killed" when a police station was attacked, denied directing or instructing the police, and said the police units that responded were not engaged in connection with Kibali's operations. Kibali told Reuters the demonstration did not take place on its concession and was not connected to the company. No court has ruled on who caused the deaths.
cases.outcome: The complainants filed against Barrick at Canada's National Contact Point on 10 May 2022. That contact point offered its good offices only on the claim that the company contributed to human rights harm from the 2021 exclusion-zone resettlement, and treated the other claims, including the police response in Durba and the tax claims, as not material or not substantiated enough; it did not publish its initial assessment, and shared the finalised assessment with the parties on 28 August 2023. After one dialogue on 1 December 2023 it concluded that further engagement was unlikely to resolve the matter. It approved its final statement on 19 April 2024, published it on 17 May 2024, said the statement should not be seen as validating either side's claims, and recommended that Barrick disclose more about its engagement with government authorities over the 2021 operation and about its relationship with local police, and keep engaging with the community. It said it would follow up with the parties six months later. A parallel complaint against AngloGold Ashanti was filed at the UK National Contact Point in 2022 and withdrawn in July 2022, because the contact point found no significant link between the company and the UK. A fresh complaint dated 5 February 2024 was formally received by the UK contact point on 22 November 2024; on 12 December 2025 it accepted six paragraphs of the OECD Guidelines for further examination, rejected the tax allegations as unsubstantiated, offered mediation to both parties, and said this does not mean it has concluded that the Guidelines were breached. On 27 July 2026 the same households filed against AngloGold Ashanti at the United States National Contact Point (OECD Watch). The governor's office suspended the evictions after the protest and opened an inquiry (Reuters). The justice minister told judicial authorities to open investigations and bring prosecutions where warranted; a year later Avocats Sans Frontières was still calling for those investigations to be sped up and asking Kibali Goldmines SA to pay compensation and help with resettlement. A claim by 1,037 self-identified residents of Bandayi against Kibali and the Congolese state was dismissed on procedural grounds by the Kinshasa/Gombe commercial tribunal in April 2022, without findings on the facts or on liability (Canada's National Contact Point).

cases.confidence_note: The demolitions, the schools lost, the injuries and the deaths are recorded outside the complaints, by a mission of three members of the national parliament whose findings PAX sets out and Mining.com reported from Reuters, and by PAX's own field research, which drew on more than 25 interviews and satellite imagery. Barrick disputes PAX's account. It says the people in Mege and Bandayi were illegal occupants of Exclusion Zone B, that Kibali moved all households inside the zone and that Mege and Bandayi were moved in September 2013, that the part of Mege and Bandayi inside the zone consisted of 26 isolated households, that the October 2021 operation was a government-run eviction of illegal occupants in which Kibali had no involvement, and that it called PAX's initial findings inaccurate; these are the company's own statements, quoted in PAX's report and in the two contact points' documents. Barrick also denies directing or controlling the local police, and Kibali told Reuters the demonstration was not on its concession and not connected to the company. The counts do not agree: PAX puts more than 2,500 houses demolished, the parliamentary mission counted 1,550 in Bandayi and 956 in Mege, and Avocats Sans Frontières counts 953 structures in Mege alone. On the deaths, the parliamentary mission counted four dead including a soldier killed by protesters, PAX's summary says at least three and one later passage refers to reports of at least four killed, Reuters's source confirmed at least one, and the complainant alleged six. Canada's National Contact Point said its statement validates neither side's claims, the UK contact point says its acceptance is not a finding that the Guidelines were breached, and the Kinshasa/Gombe commercial tribunal dismissed the residents' 2022 claim on procedural grounds without findings of fact.

cases.whole: Kibali produced its first gold bar in November 2013 and 364,000 ounces of gold in 2020, the year before the demolitions; the output figure is from the company's own website, reported by Reuters. PAX gives mining permits of 1,836 square kilometres, about 60 percent of the Haut-Uélé provincial government's revenues coming from Kibali, a dividend of US$200 million paid to shareholders in 2021, and an operating life currently projected to 2040. PAX counts more than 36,000 people relocated by the project across three resettlement campaigns since 2012. The resettlement totals are the companies' own and are disputed: Barrick said in 2022 that over 20,000 individuals from at least 4,000 households had been relocated and resettled, and in November 2024 that 16,277 project-affected people in 3,777 households had been resettled; PAX rejects Barrick's account of Mege and Bandayi. PAX found one payment reported to the Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative, US$58,501 in 2015, labelled as compensation for Mege. A year after the demolitions Avocats Sans Frontières reported 610 victims still without shelter or basic services and asked Kibali Goldmines SA to pay compensation and help with resettlement. No figure for compensation paid to the demolished households was found in the documents opened. Part of the Bandayi neighbourhood inside Exclusion Zone B has become a waste dump for Kibali's open pits (PAX).

reasoning.killed: At least four people died at the Durba protest of 22 October 2021. PAX read the parliamentary mission's report and its annexed documents from health facilities: they record a soldier killed with a blunt object, at least three other people shot dead and fourteen injured, and the report carried four death certificates and photographs of the bodies. So of the four deaths the parliamentary mission counted, one was caused by protesters and three by state security forces firing live ammunition. The project's rule counts only deaths caused by the project, the company, or forces acting for them, so the soldier is out and the count is three. The three are counted, rather than left uncounted, because the forces that fired are the same forces that carried out the demolition operation for the mine's exclusion zone, and the protest was against that operation: PAX records heavy machinery protected by state security forces, says the evictions followed repeated complaints by Kibali to the provincial and national governments and would not have been carried out without Kibali's wish to use the land, and Canada's National Contact Point recommended that Barrick disclose the nature of its relationship with local police and any arrangement to give material support to public security authorities, and that it keep engaging with the community about the role of local police in providing security for the mine site. That matches how this map has handled the same question before: three Adivasis shot by Odisha police at Maikanch are counted because the police were acting against a blockade of the project, and two deaths at a Peruvian mine are counted as police acting for the mine, while deaths are left uncounted where no source puts the forces at the project's service, as at a national wage strike in Cambodia and at a plant in Egypt where protesters had blocked a port. Higher counts are floors or allegations and stay uncounted in killed_note: Avocats Sans Frontières' at least four is the parliamentary four including the soldier, the complainant alleged six killed by police, Actualité.cd reported six, and PAX received reports of further deaths it could not confirm. Reuters's at least one, from the governor's office, is a floor and does not say who fired. Barrick's own account is two civilians and one police officer. No court has ruled on who caused the deaths, which is why the case is contested rather than documented.
reasoning.confidence: contested. Barrick disputes the record throughout: it calls the residents illegal occupants of Exclusion Zone B, says Kibali moved all households inside the zone and that Mege and Bandayi were moved in September 2013, says the part of the two villages inside the zone was 26 isolated households, says the October 2021 operation was a government eviction in which Kibali had no involvement, called PAX's initial findings inaccurate, and denies directing or controlling the local police; Kibali told Reuters the demonstration was not on its concession or connected to the company. Under this project's rule and under BRIEF45, a case the company disputes is contested, with the dispute named, and it is named in confidence_note. The harm is also recorded outside the company and outside the complaint, by the parliamentary mission and by PAX's field research, so the case meets the second test and is not a drop; but outside corroboration alone does not make it documented while the company contests the record. Neither contact point has made a finding on the facts: Canada's statement says it validates neither side's claims and the UK contact point says acceptance is not a conclusion that the Guidelines were breached.
reasoning.sources_cut: Wikipedia's Kibali Gold Mine page was cut, with the three figures that rested on it: commissioning in September 2013 after about $1.7 billion of development, 814,000 ounces produced in 2019, and the projection of 600,000 ounces a year for the first twelve years. The page does carry all three, but they are not usable here where press and primary sources exist. In their place the card uses PAX for the first gold bar in November 2013, the 1,836 square kilometres of permits, the 60 percent share of provincial revenue, the US$200 million dividend in 2021 and the projection to 2040, and Reuters for 364,000 ounces in 2020, labelled as a company website figure. The Business Wire release on the AngloGold Ashanti NYSE listing was also cut, because businesswire.com returned an empty reply to two attempts; the 25 September 2023 restructuring and primary NYSE listing are taken from the UK contact point's initial assessment instead. Mining.com returned 403 to a plain request and was read through the WebFetch route, which resolved it; its two figures are on the card. Every other figure named for checking was found in the document cited: more than 2,500 houses (PAX), 1,550 houses plus a nursery, a primary and a secondary school in Bandayi and 956 houses in Mege (PAX, reporting the parliamentary mission), more than 2,360 households (OECD Watch, all three complaint pages), 45/45/10 Barrick-AngloGold-SOKIMO (PAX, UK contact point, Canada's contact point and Reuters), and 14 wounded (PAX and Mining.com; Avocats Sans Frontières says more than fifteen).
